title: Ruffled buttercream
subtitle: layered petal effect piped with a flat petal nozzle
excerpt: Ruffled buttercream covers a cake in overlapping petals of soft buttercream, each one piped with a flat petal nozzle held at a slight angle and moved in a short arc. The technique looks complex but is repetitive once the hand motion is learned. A crumb-coated, chilled cake is essential: the surface must be firm or the ruffles will drag.
sourceNotes: Ruffle buttercream technique, widely taught in British and American cake-decorating courses from the early 2010s. Petal nozzle identification from standard Wilton and PME nozzle catalogues.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat, teardrop-shaped piping nozzle with one thin end and one thick end, used to pipe petals, ruffles, and ribbon effects.
A smooth, silky buttercream made from egg whites and sugar cooked together then whipped with butter. Holds its shape well at room temperature and pipes cleanly.

content.text: Ruffled buttercream is piped with a

held at a 45-degree angle to the cake surface and moved in a short, even arc to create overlapping petals. The motion is the same as drawing a shallow C with the tip of the nozzle. Work from the base of the cake upward, overlapping each row so the thick end of each petal covers the thin edge of the row below.
or a firm American buttercream (icing sugar plus butter). Both hold a defined edge. A very soft or greasy buttercream will not hold the ruffle shape once piped.
Fit a petal nozzle (Wilton 104 or PME equivalent) into a piping bag. Fill with firm, room-temperature buttercream. Squeeze from the top of the bag downward to remove air pockets.
Place the crumb-coated, chilled cake on a turntable. The surface must be fully firm before ruffling starts. If it gives to pressure, return it to the fridge for 15 minutes.
Hold the bag with the thin end of the nozzle pointing away from the cake and the thick end resting lightly against the surface. Angle the nozzle at about 45 degrees to the vertical.

Begin at the base of the cake. Apply even pressure and sweep the nozzle in a short arc of about 3 cm, moving it slightly up and then back down as you go, to create the petal shape. Release pressure at the end of each arc.
Move along the base in overlapping arcs, spacing them about 2 cm apart, until you have completed the first row around the whole cake.
Start the second row directly above the first, positioning the thick base of each petal to just overlap the thin edge of the row below. Continue upward until you reach the top edge.
For the top, pipe ruffles from the outer edge inward in concentric rings, or leave it plain and add a different decoration.

attrs.problem: Ruffles losing their shape and slumping
attrs.avoid: Avoid working in a warm room or with buttercream that is too soft.
attrs.fix: Chill the buttercream briefly in the piping bag, then test a ruffle on a flat surface before returning to the cake.

attrs.problem: Ruffles tearing or dragging the crumb coat
attrs.avoid: Avoid pressing the nozzle too hard against an under-chilled surface.
attrs.fix: Chill the cake for a further 20 minutes, then rework the affected section with fresh buttercream.

attrs.problem: Uneven petal size across the cake
attrs.avoid: Avoid changing hand speed mid-arc; consistent pressure gives consistent petal size.
attrs.fix: Practise the arc motion on a piece of baking paper until the size is reliably even before applying to the cake.
